items.value: It is difficult, if not impossible, to repair every manifestation of historical injustice
items.reasoning: The passage's spine is repair and its resistance: historical wrongs 'continue into the present in some form or the other and tend to resist repair', and it then gives two reasons for that resistance (roots buried deep in history plus injustice constituting whole economic, ideological and representational structures; and the category spanning many overlapping wrongs one of which acquires partial autonomy). D states exactly that difficulty, and its hedge 'if not impossible' matches the passage's 'tend to resist'. A inverts the opening sentence, which says theorists must take such history seriously, not that they have failed to. B overstates with 'inevitable' and 'always beyond repair'. C reverses the passage, which makes injustice constitutive of economic structures rather than a product of 'bad economies'.

items.value: Neither assumption is valid
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is contradicted rather than assumed: the passage says one wrong, 'generally discrimination, tends to acquire partial autonomy from others', which is precisely why removing economic deprivation would not automatically remove social discrimination. Statement 2 introduces democratic polity, a topic the passage never raises — it discusses political theorists and the history of repair, never a form of government as the best remedy. So neither assumption underlies the passage.

items.value: Only the assumption that education is incomplete without culture is valid
items.reasoning: Statement 2 is directly underwritten: 'A merely well informed man is only a bore on God's earth' and 'What we should aim at is producing men who possess both culture and expert knowledge' — information without culture is treated as an incomplete education. Statement 1 converts the passage's positive claim (education plays a great transformatory role) into a necessary condition about society ('cannot be transformed into a modern society'), which the passage never asserts; its focus throughout is the individual — 'meaning to human existence'. Runner-up C (both valid): it wins if one reads 'Education plays a great transformatory role in life, particularly so in this rapidly changing and globalizing world' as presupposing that a society cannot modernise without educated people. I set it aside because that is a strictly stronger, society-level necessity claim than the passage makes.

items.value: Only the assumption that sustainable soil management helps combat climate change is valid
items.reasoning: Statement 3 is the passage's closing point: soil 'can trap huge quantities of carbon dioxide in the form of organic carbon and prevent it from escaping into the atmosphere', so conserving soil keeps carbon out of the air. Statement 2 is decisive against the other three options — the passage names erosion and its scale but says nothing whatever about its causes, so 'mainly anthropogenic' is not assumed; every option except B contains statement 2. Statement 1 also overreaches: the passage says the loss is 'alarming — and not just for food producers', but never mentions food insecurity, still less makes erosion its major cause.

items.value: Only the assumption that economic power is better analysed through its effects than by direct measurement is valid
items.reasoning: Statement 3 restates the passage's core contrast: the power that drives inequality is 'invisible and not measurable', while 'its effects are seen in a pervasive manner in all spheres' — so effects are the available evidence. Statement 1 fails on the word 'only': power is called 'the organising principle' of inequality, which is not a claim that it is the sole cause, and the passage lists gender, race, religion and region alongside income and wealth. Statement 2 reverses the passage's direction of causation — power drives and organises inequality; the passage never says inequality reinforces power.

items.value: Farmers who modernise their methods and diversify their crops will be advantageously placed in future
items.reasoning: The passage says suitable croplands for the four commodities will shift by 2050, 'in some cases pushing farmers to plant new crops', and closes with 'Climate alone does not dictate yields; political shifts, global demand, and agricultural practices will influence how farms fare in the future.' Since practice, not climate alone, decides outcomes, the farmer who adapts and diversifies is better placed — inference A. D is directly contradicted by that closing sentence. B is unsupported: shifting croplands is not a claim about loss of crop diversity. C invents a great increase in total cultivated area, whereas the passage describes croplands shifting, with some farmlands gaining and others not.

items.value: Man and the animals named share an evolutionary history
items.reasoning: The passage's whole point is that a bat's wing, a mole's digging hand, a horse's leg, a porpoise's paddle and a human hand are 'all constructed on the same pattern' — the same five fingers, the same wrist bones, the same long arm bones, despite serving quite different functions. One underlying plan behind different uses is the signature of common ancestry, so D. A and B misapply 'biodiversity', which denotes the variety of life, not shared anatomical structure. C calls it coincidence, which is exactly what a shared bone-for-bone pattern across many species is not.

items.value: Assumptions 1 and 3 are valid: warming bears on biological evolution, and it can change the composition of flora and fauna
items.reasoning: The PETM warming brought 'drought, floods, insect plagues and a few extinctions' and left life 'drastically different' — that supports both 1 (warming bears on the planet's biological evolution) and 3 (warming can change what flora and fauna the Earth carries). Statement 2 is not made: the passage mentions that the Atlantic had not fully opened as background geography and separately attributes the warming to 'a massive geologically sudden release of carbon', with no causal link asserted between land separation and that release. Statement 4 misreads a conditional comparison — the ancient carbon was roughly what would be released if humans burned all reserves of coal, oil and gas — into a prediction that present warming will end in PETM-like conditions.

Count the digit position by position over 1 to 999. The digit 5 occupies the units place in 5, 15, 25, ... 995, which is 100 numbers; likewise 100 occurrences in the tens place (50-59, 150-159, ... 950-959) and 100 in the hundreds place (500-599). That is 3 x 100 = 300, and 1000 contains no 5. Verified by direct enumeration of 1 to 1000, which returns 300.

items.value: 8 cubes have exactly one painted face
items.reasoning: Four big and thirty-two small pieces fit only one way: the solid is 4 x 4 x 4 in unit terms, the big cubes are 2 x 2 x 2 (4 x 8 = 32 units) and the small ones are unit cubes (32 units), totalling 64. Since no big cube may show blue and blue occupies the two opposite faces at the top and bottom, each 2-cube must span the middle levels, and four of them exactly fill that middle slab; the remaining 32 unit cubes form the top and bottom layers. Every big cube then sits at a corner of the slab and shows two side faces, so none has just one. In each 4 x 4 outer layer the four central unit cubes touch only the blue face — 4 above and 4 below, giving 8. Verified by enumerating all 36 pieces: the painted-face histogram is 8 pieces with one face, 20 with two and 8 with three.

items.value: 37.5 per cent
items.reasoning: Take A as 100 units. Placing B on A raises the weight by 60 per cent, so A and B together weigh 160 and B alone is 60. The question asks for the reduction measured against the combined weight of A and B, so it is 60/160 = 3/8 = 37.5 per cent. The 60 per cent of option A is the trap: that is the increase measured against A alone, and a rise and the matching fall have different percentage values because the base changes.

items.value: Thursday
items.reasoning: April and November both have 30 days, so only the weekdays of the 1st and 2nd of the month occur five times. Five Mondays in April means 1 April is a Sunday or a Monday; five Thursdays in November means 1 November is a Wednesday or a Thursday. From 1 April to 1 November is 30+31+30+31+31+30+31 = 214 days, and 214 leaves remainder 4 on division by 7, so 1 November falls four weekdays after 1 April. Only 1 April = Sunday works, giving 1 November = Thursday. Then 1 December is Saturday (November's 30 days shift by 2) and 20 December is Thursday. Checked against every year from 1900 to 2100 that satisfies both conditions — all 29 of them put 20 December on a Thursday.

items.value: Only conclusion III follows
items.reasoning: Conclusion III is simply the converse of statement 1, and a particular affirmative converts validly: if some rats are cats, then some cats are rats. Conclusion I does not follow — 'no dog is a cow' excludes cows only from the dogs, and the cats that are not dogs are left free to be cows. Conclusion II does not follow either: the rats-cats overlap and the cats-dogs overlap need not be the same cats, but nothing forbids a rat from being a dog, so 'no dog is a rat' is not established.

A parallelogram is fixed by choosing two lines from the first parallel family and two from the second, since each pair of parallels supplies one pair of opposite sides. The count is therefore C(4,2) x C(4,2) = 6 x 6 = 36.

items.value: 8 students play both
items.reasoning: A student plays football exactly when the identification number is divisible by 4 and cricket exactly when it is divisible by 6, so playing both means the number is divisible by the least common multiple of 4 and 6, which is 12. Between 1 and 100 the multiples of 12 are 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72, 84 and 96 — eight numbers. Note 24 is the trap: the common divisor route gives no one, and using 4 x 6 = 24 would wrongly give 4.

items.value: 15 km
items.reasoning: At the 12 km mark she had completed 80 per cent of the race, so 12 is 0.8 of the full distance and the race is 12/0.8 = 15 km. A check confirms it: 80 per cent of 15 is 12.

items.value: Raju still does not have enough money to buy the handset
items.reasoning: Rupees 9000 is 75 per cent of the price, so the handset costs 9000/0.75 = 12,000. After borrowing 2000 he holds 11,000, which is 1000 short. Options C and D reverse the shortfall into a surplus; B would need the price to be exactly 11,000, whereas the stated 75 per cent fixes it at 12,000.

Let Meenu be m in 2002, so Meera is 3m. Eight years later 2(m+8) = 3m+8, giving m = 8. Meenu was therefore 8 in 2002 and born in 1994. The check works: in 2002 the ages are 8 and 24, and in 2010 they are 16 and 32, so Meenu is exactly half of Meera.

items.value: Rupees 210 per racket
items.reasoning: The individual spends are a distraction; only the total matters, since between them they bought 10 balls and 10 rackets for 1300 + 1500 = 2800. With a ball at b and a racket at 3b, the total is 10b + 30b = 40b = 2800, so b = 70 and a racket costs 210. Option A (70) is the price of a ball, offered as the trap.

items.value: Both statements are correct
items.reasoning: With 70 Indians and 60 vegetarians among 100 people, the overlap is at least 70 + 60 - 100 = 30, so statement 1 holds. There are 40 non-vegetarians and only 30 non-Indians, so at least 40 - 30 = 10 non-vegetarians must be Indian, and statement 2 holds. Both bounds are tight and both are guaranteed: enumerating all 31 consistent tables gives Indian vegetarians ranging from 30 to 60 and Indian non-vegetarians never below 10.

items.value: As we go digital we must recognise the huge threat to Internet security posed by some IoT devices
items.reasoning: The passage is built entirely around one tension: low-end IoT devices are cheap commodities on which 'addressing security would add to the cost', the class 'is proliferating', the IoT 'is expected to expand exponentially — but new security challenges are daunting.' D is that warning. A and B both name India, which the passage never mentions. C picks up the convenience of the devices, but comfort is incidental scene-setting here, not the message the passage is organised to deliver.

items.value: India should be careful to protect its digital sovereignty in global trade talks
items.reasoning: The passage's first sentence is that global trade negotiations are 'eyeing the digital area in an attempt to pre-emptively colonise it', and it then describes data being freely mined from developing countries and turned into rent-extracting intelligence elsewhere. Guarding one's digital space precisely in those trade negotiations is the direct corollary. A condemns globalisation wholesale, which the passage does not. C would have India join in extracting monopoly rents, which is the practice being criticised, not a remedy. D asserts a proportionality between data loss and the value of foreign trade that appears nowhere in the text.

items.value: Big Data is the key resource in the digital space
items.reasoning: The cab-service example is the clincher: such a company 'is not a network of cars and drivers; it is digital intelligence' about commuting, roads, traffic and personal behaviour. The passage thus treats data, not physical assets, as the thing that carries value, is 'mined', and yields control of sectors and monopoly rents — that is what makes it the key resource, and it is the premise the rest of the argument rests on. B is contradicted, since Big Data is drawn from developing countries. C fails on 'prerogative', which asserts an exclusive right the passage never grants. Runner-up D ('access to and possession of Big Data is a characteristic of developed countries'): it wins if 'most definitively implied' is read as asking for the proposition closest to the literal text, since the passage does say the data is converted into intelligence in developed countries. I set it aside because 'is a characteristic of' makes a defining claim about developed countries that the passage does not, and because the passage's point is the flow of data rather than a property of one group.

items.value: Supporting small farmers is an important part of any environmentally sustainable development agenda
items.reasoning: The passage puts the rural poor on the frontline of a climate change they did little to cause, then establishes the weight of small farms — two billion people depend on them worldwide and India's small-holders produce 41 per cent of the country's food grains. Helping that group is therefore central to any sustainable development agenda. B is contradicted by the passage's insistence that the poor are on the frontline of coping. C turns a vulnerability into a guarantee of food security. D fails on 'only': 41 per cent is a large share, not the whole, so small-holders alone cannot be said to ensure food security.

items.value: Both implications are valid
items.reasoning: Implication 1 follows: India's small-holders supply 41 per cent of its food grains and are exactly the group whose rainfall and temperature assumptions no longer hold, so there is a potential food-insecurity problem. Implication 2 follows from the passage's own catalogue of hazards — 'more frequent and extreme weather events, such as droughts and floods, can spell disaster', plus sea level rise and glacier melt affecting water supply; a country facing more frequent disasters must strengthen its capacity to manage them. Runner-up A (1 only): it wins on a strict reading, since the passage describes farmers coping and never mentions the state's disaster machinery, so 'disaster management capabilities' could be judged an outside prescription. I chose C because the passage names the disasters and their rising frequency explicitly, which makes the need to prepare for them an implication rather than an import.
